claim: Leptospirosis affects millions of people worldwide causing an overall mortality rate of 65,000 per year.
source: Leptospirosis, a neglected re-emerging enzootic spirochetal disease, affects millions of people worldwide causing an overall mortality rate of 65,000 per year (Costa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Costa et al., 2015.

claim: Leptospirosis causes serious health problems in animals of agricultural interest which leads to substantial economic losses mostly in tropical and subtropical countries.
source: In addition, it causes serious health problems in animals of agricultural interest which leads to substantial economic losses mostly in tropical and subtropical countries.
evidence: This is a statement drawing from established knowledge about leptospirosis impacts.

claim: Assessing the true severity of leptospirosis can be incredibly challenging, especially when early diagnosis is difficult due to nonspecific symptoms that overlap with other illnesses.
source: Assessing the true severity of leptospirosis can be incredibly challenging, especially when early diagnosis is difficult due to nonspecific symptoms that overlap with other illnesses (Haake and Levett, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Haake and Levett, 2015.

claim: Recent outbreaks of both human and canine leptospirosis occurred in New York and California in 2020–2022.
source: Recent outbreaks of both human and canine leptospirosis in New York and California in 2020–2022 (NYC Health, 2021; Health, 2022) underscores the need for development of effective strategies to control this disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to NYC Health, 2021 and Health, 2022.

claim: No broadly effective vaccine is available for either humans or animals against leptospirosis.
source: Although serovar-specific vaccines are available for animals and at least one is available for humans, no broadly effective vaccine is available for either (Barazzone et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barazzone et al., 2021.

claim: The genus Leptospira is broadly categorized into two major clades P and S (Pathogens and Saprophytes).
source: The genus Leptospira is broadly categorized into two major clades P and S (Pathogens and Saprophytes) and further categorized into four subclades, P1, P2, S1, and S2 based on their virulence properties, growth conditions, and genetic make-up (Vincent et al., 2019; Picardeau, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vincent et al., 2019 and Picardeau, 2017.

claim: Leptospira is further categorized into four subclades, P1, P2, S1, and S2 based on their virulence properties, growth conditions, and genetic make-up.
source: The genus Leptospira is broadly categorized into two major clades P and S (Pathogens and Saprophytes) and further categorized into four subclades, P1, P2, S1, and S2 based on their virulence properties, growth conditions, and genetic make-up (Vincent et al., 2019; Picardeau, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vincent et al., 2019 and Picardeau, 2017.

claim: Subclade P1 is divided into two phylogenetically related groups named P1+ (high-virulence pathogens) and P1- (low-virulence pathogens).
source: Subclade P1 is further divided in two phylogenetically related groups named P1+ (high-virulence pathogens, established pathogenic species, e.g. Leptospira interrogans) and P1- (low-virulence pathogens, phenotypically not well characterized) (Giraud-Gatineau et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Giraud-Gatineau et al., 2024.

claim: Leptospira interrogans is an example of a high-virulence pathogen in the P1+ group.
source: Subclade P1 is further divided in two phylogenetically related groups named P1+ (high-virulence pathogens, established pathogenic species, e.g. Leptospira interrogans) and P1- (low-virulence pathogens, phenotypically not well characterized) (Giraud-Gatineau et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Giraud-Gatineau et al., 2024.

claim: Leptospira survives in moist conditions and are free-living organisms naturally found in soil and water.
source: Leptospira survives in moist conditions and are free-living organisms naturally found in soil and water (Narkkul et al., 2020; Benacer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Narkkul et al., 2020 and Benacer et al., 2013.

claim: The spread of leptospirosis infection occurs through contaminated water contact with breached skin or mucosal surfaces.
source: The spread of infection occurs through contaminated water contact with breached skin or mucosal surfaces (Ko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ko et al., 2009.

claim: Saprophytic strains of Leptospira, such as Leptospira biflexa, are unable to establish disease due to the lack of certain virulence factors.
source: Saprophytic strains of Leptospira, such as Leptospira biflexa (S1), are unable to establish disease due to the lack of certain virulence factors (Picardeau, 2017) and have been found in natural environments around the world alongside pathogenic serovars (Vincent et al., 2019; Ko et al., 2009; Guglielmini et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Picardeau, 2017.

claim: Saprophytic Leptospira have been found in natural environments around the world alongside pathogenic serovars.
source: Saprophytic strains of Leptospira, such as Leptospira biflexa (S1), are unable to establish disease due to the lack of certain virulence factors (Picardeau, 2017) and have been found in natural environments around the world alongside pathogenic serovars (Vincent et al., 2019; Ko et al., 2009; Guglielmini et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vincent et al., 2019, Ko et al., 2009, and Guglielmini et al., 2019.

claim: L. biflexa exhibits certain niche-specific adaptations that allow them to persist in both environmental and host settings.
source: Moreover, L. biflexa exhibits certain niche-specific adaptations that allow them to persist in both environmental and host settings (Zhang et al., 2018; Castiblanco-Valencia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2018 and Castiblanco-Valencia et al., 2016.

claim: L. biflexa triggers a robust innate immune response in mice during the acute phase of infection.
source: Our previous studies (Shetty et al., 2021; Kundu et al., 2022) demonstrated that L. biflexa triggers a robust innate immune response in mice during the acute phase of infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous studies (Shetty et al., 2021; Kundu et al., 2022).

claim: Mice inoculated with a single dose of L. biflexa 2 weeks before challenge with L. interrogans showed significant rescue of weight loss compared to mice that did not receive L. biflexa.
source: We inoculated adult C3H-HeJ male mice with a single dose of L. biflexa 2 weeks before challenge with L. interrogans (LB1LIC1) at 8 weeks (Figure 1A) and measured a significant rescue of weight loss over a period of 15 days as compared to mice infected at 8 weeks that did not receive L. biflexa (PBS1LIC1) (p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing statistical significance (p<0.0001) and is illustrated in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: 75% of mice that received one dose of L. biflexa before challenge with L. interrogans survived, compared to 0% survival in mice that did not receive L. biflexa.
source: All mice infected with L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1) reached the 20% weight loss endpoint criteria between d9 and d12 post infection. In contrast, 75% of the mice that received one dose of L. biflexa before challenge with L. interrogans (LB1LIC1) survived and gained significant body weight (Figure 1B) which was similar to the naïve control that received only PBS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental survival data presented in the text and Figure 1C.

claim: A single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood.
source: We also found that a single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent shedding of L. interrogans in urine.
source: We also found that a single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or shedding in urine (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent kidney colonization by L. interrogans.
source: We also found that a single exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or shedding in urine (Figure 1D), or kidney colonization (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Culture of kidney from LB1LIC1 mice showed presence of ~2500 motile, morphologically intact L. interrogans on d3 and d5 post culture.
source: Culture of kidney in EMJH media showed presence of ~2500 motile, morphologically intact L. interrogans under dark-field microscopy which was confirmed by 16S qPCR (Figure 1F) both on d3 and d5 post culture of kidney collected from LB1LIC1 mice
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-field microscopy and qPCR shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mice inoculated with two bi-weekly doses of L. biflexa 2 weeks before challenge with L. interrogans lost a maximum of 5% weight on d10 and recovered fully by d15 post infection.
source: In contrast, mice that received a double dose of L. biflexa 2 weeks before challenge at 10 weeks with L. interrogans (LB2LIC2) lost a maximum of 5% weight on d10 and recovered fully by d15 post infection
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental weight measurement data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All experimental groups in the double exposure study survived LIC infection.
source: Survival curves generated after the mice reached endpoint criteria (Figure 2C) show that all experimental groups survived LIC infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood.
source: Analysis of bacterial dissemination showed that a double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent shedding of L. interrogans in urine.
source: Analysis of bacterial dissemination showed that a double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), or shedding in urine (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent kidney colonization by L. interrogans.
source: Analysis of bacterial dissemination showed that a double exposure to L. biflexa before challenge did not prevent dissemination of pathogenic L. interrogans in blood (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), or shedding in urine (Figure 2D), or kidney colonization (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Culture of kidney from PBS2LIC2 mice showed presence of 5000–10,000 motile, morphologically intact L. interrogans on d3 and d5 post culture.
source: Culture of kidney in EMJH media showed presence of 5000–10,000 motile, morphologically intact L. interrogans on d3 and d5 post culture of kidney collected from PBS2LIC2 mice
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-field microscopy and qPCR shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Culture of kidney from LB2LIC2 mice showed presence of 1000–2500 live L. interrogans.
source: in contrast to 1000–2500 live L. interrogans observed in culture from kidney collected from LB2LIC2 mice which was confirmed by 16S qPCR (Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-field microscopy and qPCR shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1 and PBS2LIC2) showed signs of inflammation with increased immune cell infiltration.
source: As expected, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of histological slices of all kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans in both single and double exposure experiments (PBS1LIC1 and PBS2LIC2) showed signs of inflammation with increased immune cell infiltration (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: Kidneys from mice exposed to L. biflexa before L. interrogans challenge (LB1LIC1 and LB2LIC2) showed reduced immune cell infiltration.
source: In contrast, H&E staining of kidney slices from the groups of mice exposed to L. biflexa before L. interrogans challenge (LB1LIC1 and LB2LIC2) showed reduced immune cell infiltration.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: Kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1 and PBS2LIC2) had significantly higher expression of ColA1 compared to controls.
source: In both experiments, kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1 and PBS2LIC2) had significantly higher expression of ColA1 as compared to the controls
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans after exposure to L. biflexa (LB1LIC1 and LB2LIC2) had ColA1 expression not different than controls.
source: in contrast, kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans after exposure to L. biflexa (LB1LIC1 and LB2LIC2) were not different than the controls (Figure 3B and D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Kidneys from LB2LIC2 mice maintained their normal gross anatomy and coloration as did kidneys from control mice.
source: We found that kidney from LB2LIC2 mice maintained their normal gross anatomy and coloration as did kidneys from control mice (PBS2 and LB2), in contrast to kidneys from mice challenged with L. interrogans that were not previously exposed to L. biflexa (PBS2LIC2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gross morphological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: IgG2a antibodies against L. interrogans were significantly higher in mice pre-exposed to L. biflexa before challenge with L. interrogans in both single and double exposure experiments.
source: Our data also shows that prior exposure to non-pathogenic Leptospira before pathogenic challenge induced higher antibody titer in the serum, specifically IgG2a antibodies against L. interrogans in both single and double exposure experiments (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: IgG2a differences between PBS1/2LIC1/2 and LB1/2LIC1/2 groups were significant (p=0.001 for single exposure and p=0.0095 for double exposure).
source: Although differences between groups (PBS2v PBS2LIC2 and LB1/2 vs LB1/2LIC1/2) were significant, differences between the LIC infected groups (PBS1/2LIC1/2 vs LB1/2LIC1/2) were not significant for IgG1 and for IgG3 in contrast to IgG2a (p=0.001 for single exposure and p=0.0095 for double exposure) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ELISA data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increased IgG2a response in serum is associated with induction of a Th1 biased immune response.
source: Increased IgG2a response in serum is associated with induction of a Th1 biased immune response.
evidence: This is a statement based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Saprophytic L. biflexa induced Th1 responses, higher T cell proliferation, and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells.
source: Others have recently found that saprophytic L. biflexa induced Th1 responses, higher T cell proliferation, and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells (Krangvichian et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krangvichian et al., 2023.

claim: Frequency of B cells was increased when LIC infected mice were compared to the respective controls, but not between PBS2LIC2 and LB2LIC2 mice.
source: In the L. biflexa double exposure experiment, we measured increased frequencies in B cells when LIC infected mice were compared to the respective controls, but not between PBS2LIC2 and LB2LIC2 mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Frequency of T cells was decreased when LIC infected mice were compared to the respective controls but not between PBS2LIC2 and LB2LIC2 mice.
source: We measured decreased frequencies in T cells when LIC infected mice were compared to the respective controls but not between PBS2LIC2 and LB2LIC2 mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No differences were observed in NK cells between any of the groups in the double exposure experiment.
source: No differences were observed in NK cells between any of the groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Frequency of helper T cells was increased between all groups, with PBS2LIC2 vs LB2LIC2 p=0.006.
source: We measured increased frequencies in helper T cells between all groups; of note, PBS2LIC2 vs LB2LIC2 p=0.006 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Frequency of cytotoxic T cells was decreased between all groups, with PBS2LIC2 vs LB2LIC2 p=0.0056.
source: We also measured decreased frequencies in cytotoxic T cells between all groups; of note PBS2LIC2 vs LB2LIC2 p=0.0056 (Figure 5E; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Frequency of early effector CD4+ T helper cells was significantly increased when compared between the LIC challenged groups and the respective controls.
source: Furthermore, T cell subset typing (Figure 6) showed that frequency of early effector CD4+ T helper cells (Figure 6B, CD44-CD62L-) and effector T helper cells (Figure 6C, CD44+CD62L-) were significantly increased when compared between the LIC challenged groups and the respective controls (except PBS2 vs PBS2LIC2 early effectors)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Frequency of effector T helper cells was significantly increased when compared between the LIC challenged groups and the respective controls.
source: Furthermore, T cell subset typing (Figure 6) showed that frequency of early effector CD4+ T helper cells (Figure 6B, CD44-CD62L-) and effector T helper cells (Figure 6C, CD44+CD62L-) were significantly increased when compared between the LIC challenged groups and the respective controls (except PBS2 vs PBS2LIC2 early effectors)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Frequency of early effector and effector T helper cells was higher in the LB2LIC2 group than PBS2LIC2.
source: and that frequency of early effector and effector T helper cells was higher in the LB2LIC2 group than PBS2LIC2.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: No major changes were measured in memory CD4+ T helper cells.
source: No major changes were measured in memory CD4+ T helper cells (Figure 6D, CD44+CD62L+).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Significant decreases in frequency of naïve CD8+ T cells were measured between LIC infected groups and the respective controls.
source: In the CD8+ cytotoxic T cell subsets, we measured significant decreases in frequency of naïve T cells between LIC infected groups and the respective controls (Figure 6E, CD62L+CD44-)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The likelihood of humans or animals getting exposed to non-pathogenic serovars of Leptospira is likely high given their widespread presence in nature.
source: Given their widespread presence in nature, the likelihood of humans or animals getting exposed to non-pathogenic serovars of Leptospira is likely high (Benacer et al., 2013; Ko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benacer et al., 2013 and Ko et al., 2009.

claim: L. biflexa extracts can be used to detect Leptospira-specific antibody in up to 67% of serum from patients with clinically confirmed leptospirosis.
source: In addition, L. biflexa extracts can be used to detect Leptospira-specific antibody in up to 67% of serum from patients with clinically confirmed leptospirosis (Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022) which points to a high degree of immunodominant cross-reactive epitopes between L. biflexa and pathogenic Leptospira.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022.

claim: There is a high degree of immunodominant cross-reactive epitopes between L. biflexa and pathogenic Leptospira.
source: In addition, L. biflexa extracts can be used to detect Leptospira-specific antibody in up to 67% of serum from patients with clinically confirmed leptospirosis (Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022) which points to a high degree of immunodominant cross-reactive epitopes between L. biflexa and pathogenic Leptospira.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ability of L. biflexa extracts to detect antibodies in patients with leptospirosis.

claim: The current hypothesis regarding evolution of Leptospira species is that symbiosis of Leptospira with eukaryotes emerged from free-living ancestral species.
source: Further, the current hypothesis regarding evolution of Leptospira species is that symbiosis of Leptospira with eukaryotes emerged from free-living ancestral species (Thibeaux et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thibeaux et al., 2018.

claim: Pathogenic Leptospira may have evolved from an environmental ancestor.
source: in other words, pathogenic Leptospira may have evolved from an environmental ancestor (Vincent et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vincent et al., 2019.

claim: Prior exposure to one or two doses of saprophytic L. biflexa rescues weight loss in mice challenged with pathogenic L. interrogans.
source: In the initial analysis of pathogenesis (Figure 1, Figure 2) we observed that prior exposure to one or two doses of saprophytic L. biflexa rescues weight loss in mice challenged with pathogenic L. interrogans at 8 weeks (LB1LIC1) and at 10 weeks (LB2LIC2), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Weight gain correlated with survival (75% survival in LB1LIC1 vs 0% survival of the PBS1LIC1 group) in the single exposure experiment.
source: Weight gain correlated with survival (75% survival in LB1LIC1 vs 0% survival of the PBS1LIC1 group) in the single exposure experiment
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: All mice infected at 8 weeks with pathogenic L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1) were expected to irreversibly lose weight and meet endpoint criteria for euthanasia before the 2-week term of the experiment.
source: where we expected all mice infected at 8 weeks with pathogenic L. interrogans (PBS1LIC1) to irreversibly lose weight and meet endpoint criteria for euthanasia before the 2-week term of the experiment (Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022, Shetty et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022 and Shetty et al., 2022.

claim: Loss of mice due to irreversible weight loss is not expected if mice are infected with LIC at 10 weeks of age.
source: Loss of mice due to irreversible weight loss is not expected if mice are infected with LIC at 10 weeks of age (Nair et al., 2020), as observed in the L. interrogans control group in the double exposure experiment (PBS2LIC2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nair et al., 2020.

claim: Exposure to a saprophytic Leptospira before challenge supported normal structural morphology and prevented infiltration of immune cells in kidney in both single and double exposure experiments.
source: Histological inspection of kidney slices (Figure 3) showed that exposure to a saprophytic Leptospira before challenge supported normal structural morphology and prevented infiltration of immune cells in both single and double exposure experiments
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Exposure to a saprophytic Leptospira before challenge significantly reduced a fibrosis marker (ColA1) in the single exposure experiment.
source: in addition, it significantly reduced a fibrosis marker (ColA1) in the single exposure experiment.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 10-week-old C3H-HeJ mice infected with LIC are more resistant to pathology resultant from infection.
source: In the double exposure experiment, differences in ColA1 fibrosis marker are not significant between the two LIC infected groups because 10-week-old C3H-HeJ infected with LIC are more resistant to pathology resultant from infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and age-related resistance.

claim: Prior exposure to non-pathogenic Leptospira before pathogenic challenge may confer protection against kidney fibrosis.
source: Our findings are intriguing as they suggest that while prior live saprophytic exposure did not prevent infection or leptospiral dissemination, it may confer protection against kidney fibrosis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Saprophytic L. biflexa induced Th1 responses, higher T cell proliferation, and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells.
source: Others have recently found that saprophytic L. biflexa induced Th1 responses, higher T cell proliferation, and IFN-γ producing CD4+ T cells (Krangvichian et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krangvichian et al., 2023.

claim: Persistent IgM and strain-specific IgG responses were observed during a homologous leptospiral challenge in C57BL6/J mice.
source: Persistent IgM and strain-specific IgG responses were observed during a homologous leptospiral challenge in C57BL6/J mice (Vernel-Pauillac et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vernel-Pauillac et al., 2021.

claim: Exposure to a saprophytic Leptospira induced antibody responses that may provide heterologous protection against the pathogenic strain of Leptospira.
source: In our study, exposure to a saprophytic Leptospira induced antibody responses that may provide heterologous protection against the pathogenic strain of Leptospira.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Live vaccines derived from a saprophytic strain of Leptospira could offer broader protection and overcome the limitation of serovar specificity often observed with killed whole-cell vaccines based on pathogenic strains.
source: Thus, live vaccines derived from a saprophytic strain of Leptospira could offer broader protection and overcome the limitation of serovar specificity often observed with killed whole-cell vaccines based on pathogenic strains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the study findings.

claim: Presence of effector helper T (CD4+) cells in the spleen indicate a robust cellular immune response.
source: Presence of effector helper T (CD4+) cells in the spleen indicate a robust cellular immune response as these cells produce cytokines that play a pivotal role in activating other immune cells, including antibody-producing B cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Components (polar lipids) derived from saprophytic L. biflexa could play a crucial role in inducing robust B cell responses.
source: Moreover, our findings align with another observation which further reinforces the potential immunostimulatory properties of components (polar lipids) derived from saprophytic L. biflexa, indicating that these components could play a crucial role in inducing robust B cell responses (Faisal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faisal et al., 2009.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells during Leptospira infection provide protective immunity to the host and mitigate the severity of leptospirosis by releasing cytokines.
source: Previous studies have highlighted the significance of activated CD4+ T cells during Leptospira infection in providing protective immunity to the host and mitigating the severity of leptospirosis by releasing cytokines (Volz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2015.

claim: Other researchers have explored vaccination strategies using live attenuated or mutant strains of pathogenic serovars.
source: While other researchers have explored vaccination strategies using live attenuated or mutant strains of pathogenic serovars, our approach was to utilize a live saprophytic bacterial strain which is unique in the field (Wunder et al., 2021; Potula et al., 2017; Lauretti-Ferreira et al., 2020; Teixeira et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wunder et al., 2021, Potula et al., 2017, Lauretti-Ferreira et al., 2020, and Teixeira et al., 2019.

claim: The approach of utilizing a live saprophytic bacterial strain for vaccination is unique in the field.
source: While other researchers have explored vaccination strategies using live attenuated or mutant strains of pathogenic serovars, our approach was to utilize a live saprophytic bacterial strain which is unique in the field (Wunder et al., 2021; Potula et al., 2017; Lauretti-Ferreira et al., 2020; Teixeira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach, supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: Oral delivery of a probiotic strain, Lactobacillus plantarum, reduces the severity of leptospirosis by recruiting myeloid cells.
source: We previously showed that oral delivery of a probiotic strain, Lactobacillus plantarum, reduces the severity of leptospirosis by recruiting myeloid cells (Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022) which suggests that a general phenomenon of trained immunity may be involved.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022.

claim: A general phenomenon of trained immunity may be involved in protection against leptospirosis.
source: We previously showed that oral delivery of a probiotic strain, Lactobacillus plantarum, reduces the severity of leptospirosis by recruiting myeloid cells (Fortes-Gabriel et al., 2022) which suggests that a general phenomenon of trained immunity may be involved.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cited study.

claim: Current vaccines based on inactivated pathogenic species provide equivalent protection to the one achieved in this study.
source: Current vaccines based on inactivated pathogenic species provide equivalent protection to the one achieved in this study (Barazzone et al., 2021; Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018) with the caveat of being serovar-specific (Teixeira et al., 2019; Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018; Adler, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barazzone et al., 2021 and Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018.

claim: Current vaccines based on inactivated pathogenic species have the caveat of being serovar-specific.
source: Current vaccines based on inactivated pathogenic species provide equivalent protection to the one achieved in this study (Barazzone et al., 2021; Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018) with the caveat of being serovar-specific (Teixeira et al., 2019; Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018; Adler, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Teixeira et al., 2019, Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018, and Adler, 2015.

claim: It remains to be shown if protection extends to multiple pathogenic serovars of Leptospira.
source: Although our current study conclusively shows protection from severe leptospirosis after heterologous challenge, it remains to be shown if protection extends to multiple pathogenic serovars of Leptospira.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation and future research direction.

claim: Using a live saprophytic strain of Leptospira as control strategy could pave the way for development of novel broadly effective vaccines against leptospirosis.
source: Using a live saprophytic strain of Leptospira as control strategy could pave the way for development of novel broadly effective vaccines against leptospirosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Such a vaccine could have a substantial economic impact if applied to animals of agricultural interest.
source: Such a vaccine could have a substantial economic impact if applied to animals of agricultural interest.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential economic impact.

claim: In the real-life scenario where individuals or animals may naturally encounter a saprophytic Leptospira species, they may develop immune responses that mitigate severe disease outcomes if the host later encounters a pathogenic strain of Leptospira.
